verification_vocabulary: As GRAPH-FORMAT.md and the settler-colonialism packet: bibliographic_metadata_checked = identity/edition checked in a catalogue or DOI record; supporting_page_checked = an abstract, contents page, publisher description or opening text was read for the specific point in `supports`; unverified = not cited. No book was read in full. Dissertation counts are 2009-2026 strict History PhDs (in_analysis) citing the matched graph work(s), not citations.

sections.precursors: National and economic histories that made the fur trade and the West a Canadian subject before Indigenous people were treated as historical actors.
sections.fur_trade_society: Fur-trade economies, families and Métis peoples, 1970s onward.
sections.contact_ethnohistory: Contact, representation and the Wendat/Huron, written across history, archaeology and anthropology.
sections.policy_institutions: Syntheses of policy and relations; reserves, residential schools, health, missions and labour.
sections.critique: Critiques of the field and its framing, from inside the field and from Indigenous scholars.
sections.historiography: Essays that survey how Canadian historians wrote about Indigenous peoples.

verification.note: Citation confirmed. The essay itself is unread. Its targets and charge are taken from answers/verification.json Q55: J. R. Miller's Reflections on Native-Newcomer Relations, seen only as a search snippet, names Cole and Chaikin, An Iron Hand upon the People (1990), Miller's 'Owen Glendower, Hotspur, and Canadian Indian Policy' and Loo's 'Dan Cranmer's Potlatch' (CHR 1992), and reports the charge that stressing agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence and so trivialised colonial harm. records.citation: Donald L. Fixico, "American Indian History and Writing from Home: Constructing an Indian Perspective," American Indian Quarterly 33, no. 4 (2009): 553–560.

verification.checked_against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex opening text
verification.note: Opening read: if the typical premise of American Indian history is the history of Indian–white relations, the ‘other side of the coin’ must be turned over to understand an Indian point of view and ‘writing from home’ by American Indian historians; oral tradition conveys ‘experiences’ rather than ‘events’. records.supports: An Indigenous historian’s critique of ‘Indian–white relations’ as a premise.

records.citation: Winona Stevenson [Wheeler], 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History', Saskatchewan History 50, no. 2 (Fall 1998): 24–27.

verification.checked_against: Open-access issue PDF on iPortal (https://iportal.usask.ca/sites/iportal.usask.ca/files/content/68012/SKHistory_Vol50_No2.pdf), pp. 24–27 read in full via OCR (answers/research/q54-indigenous-critique.json)
verification.note: Open-access issue PDF (scan) read in full via OCR, pp. 24–27. Argues that 'Indian–White Relations' historians, by relying on the remnants left by one side, keep even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and 'other' Indigenous oral histories. The author note states that she is Cree and a member of Fisher River Cree First Nation. Dated Fall 1998, not 1999. Parts II–III and her 2000 dissertation are not checked and not cited.

records.supports: A pre-2000 Canadian Indigenous critique of the 'Indian–White relations' framing: dependence on one side's documents keeps even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and sets oral history aside.
